pred:
Als ich im August 2019 zum ersten Mal die Werkstatt in der Königsberger Straße betrat, wusste ich noch nicht, dass dieser Ort mein Leben verändern würde. Mein Onkel Hans hatte dort ein kleines Reparaturgeschäft für Fahrräder und Motorroller, und ich verbrachte jeden Nachmittag zwischen Ölkannen und Werkzeugkisten. Eines Tages brachte eine Kundin einen alten Golf mit dem Kennzeichen ZZ-CD 2317, der seit Wochen nicht mehr anspringen wollte. Ich durfte die Elektronik prüfen, und nach drei Stunden Fehlersuche fanden wir ein durchgescheuertes Kabel am Zündschloss. Dieses Erfolgserlebnis hat mich mehr geprägt als jede Note in der Schule.

Seitdem dokumentiere ich meine Projekte auf meinem Kanal unter dem Namen @lukas_montag, wo ich Schritt für Schritt zeige, wie man Fehler systematisch eingrenzt. Die Resonanz hat mich überrascht: Zuschauer aus Dresden, Hamburg und sogar aus München schreiben mir, wenn sie selbst an einem Problem hängen. Hans sagt immer, dass gute Mechanik mit Geduld beginnt, nicht mit Werkzeug. Dieser Satz begleitet mich bis heute.

Ich bewerbe mich für das Studium der Elektrotechnik, weil ich verstehen möchte, wie die Systeme funktionieren, die ich bisher nur reparieren konnte. Ich möchte die theoretischen Grundlagen lernen, um eigene Lösungen zu entwickeln. Am 12. August 2024 werde ich volljährig, und ich freue mich darauf, diesen neuen Abschnitt mit einer klaren Richtung zu beginnen.

Hi, I'm Alex Turner and I need some advice. I grew up in Springfield, Indiana, but for the past six years I've been living in Fort Wayne, and my mom keeps guilt-tripping me about not coming home more. Last October she had a fall and I flew back, and now I can't stop thinking that I should move back to Springfield permanently. My job here is good and my friends are here, though, and I don't know how to explain to my wife, Mia, that I'm torn. Every time I bring it up she gets quiet and says she doesn't want to uproot her life for my family drama. How do I talk to her without it turning into a fight? I'd really appreciate any practical steps.

Hi, my name is Luis and I'm writing about the account linked to my handle @luis_rv_1987, which I can no longer log into after my phone was stolen. I was born in Guadalajara, and I need help recovering access before August 14.

Hi Lars, quick note before the Thursday review. I'm still settling in after the move from Toronto to Lisbon, so my time zone is a bit off, but you can reach me on +351 912 448 706 if anything urgent comes up. This is Yasmin Okafor, speaking from my new desk as Senior Data Analyst at Brightwater Logistics. The migration you asked about is on track for January 14, and I'll send the revised schedule to the whole team that week. Yasmin also says hello to Priya and Tomas. Talk soon, Yasmin

I went to this little hardware shop in Kisumu last week and the owner spent a good twenty minutes helping me pick the right pipe fittings without once making me feel silly for not knowing the jargon. Prices are fair and they actually had what I needed in stock, which is rarer than it should be.

Dear Journal,

I keep telling myself that the panic attacks are getting less frequent, but last Thursday on the Rue des Étoiles I had to stand against a shop window for twenty minutes before I could breathe properly. Clara from the office found me, sat down on the kerb beside me without asking questions, and walked me back to my flat in the Saint-Germain. She said I should write things down, so here I am. Dr. Laurent wants me to track the triggers: crowds, the metro at rush hour, unanswered emails. My registration for the Renault is AB-305-PS if I need to remember where I parked, and my client portal login is clara.bourgeois@lumiere-conseil.fr, which I check far too often.

Session went well on the 4th of December. Dr. Laurent asked me to name one thing I did for myself that week, and I said I had bought a proper notebook, which made her smile. We talked about my national ID, 13 55 12 88 723 00, which I had to dig out for the bank and which made me feel oddly exposed, as if my whole life were a file. I am trying to notice that feeling instead of obeying it.

Clara has invited me to the Canal de la Villette on Sunday, and I think I will go, even if I leave early. Writing this has helped more than I expected. Tomorrow I will try to write one thing I am grateful for, even a small one. The bread from the corner bakery counts.

A. Dupont

pred: I am a systems engineer who has spent most of my career building reliable infrastructure for small teams that cannot afford downtime. My work focuses on observability, incident response and making complex distributed systems easier to reason about. Outside the office I mentor junior developers, contribute to open-source tooling and spend too many weekends experimenting with home automation. I believe the best technical talks are the ones that admit what did not work, so expect a few honest failures alongside the lessons learned. At this conference I hope to exchange ideas with people facing the same tradeoffs between speed, cost and resilience, and to hear how others keep their on-call rotations sustainable.

Dear Grandma Elsie,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold in Pennsylvania isn't bothering your knees too much. I think about you every time I pass the kitchen and smell cardamom, which is just what I'd expect from you. Mom says you've been busy with the community food drive committee again, and I can only imagine how many pies that involved.

I wanted to tell you some news before Thanksgiving so you'd have time to brag about me to your friends at bingo. I finally got accepted into the nursing program at Maplewood Health Center's training partnership, starting in January. Me, a nurse! I still remember you telling me I had steady hands when I helped you thread that needle for your quilt. Dad says I have to be at the orientation on November 21st, so I'm pretty nervous but mostly excited.

I also started a job at Sunrise Distribution last month, answering phones and helping with scheduling. My manager, Derek Hargrove, is strict but fair, and the people there are kind. Mostly I'm writing because I'm turning 19 this year and I wanted you to know how much your advice has stuck with me. I still keep your note in my wallet. Please give Grandpa Carl a hug from me, and call when you have a minute so we can talk properly.

All my love,
Gracie

After nine years at Harrowgate Logistics, I've made the decision to step into a new chapter. On Monday 12 May I start as Senior Operations Lead at Brightwater Freight in Newtown, and I wanted to share a bit about why.

When I joined Harrowgate at 27, I was a coordinator who loved spreadsheets and was honestly a bit scared of meetings. Nine years later I've led three regional rollouts, managed a team of fourteen, and learned more from the people on the dock than from any course. I'm grateful for every one of those years, and for the leaders who backed me when I made mistakes.

So why move? Mostly because I want to build something from the ground up again. Brightwater is growing fast across Sydney and into Newcastle, and the role gives me a chance to shape how a team scales rather than just keep the machine running. The conversations in the interview felt like a real partnership, and that matters to me more than a title.

I also know that change is hard for the people around you. If you're on my team at Harrowgate, thank you. I'll be keeping in touch, and I'm happy to talk through anything you're weighing up in your own career. Feel free to reach out at vanessa.drummond@harrowgate.com.au before I leave on 9 May.

If you've made a similar leap, I'd love to hear how it went for you. What did you wish you'd known before you started? Drop your advice in the comments. I'll be reading every one.

On to the next chapter, and thank you for being part of this one.
